acts.title: The parking meter argument
text: The council has launched a ___ to charge drivers according to how much their car pollutes.
The stated aim is to give people an ___ to change what they drive.
Drivers’ groups have put a great deal of ___ on the council to drop it.

Anybody driving a ___ will pay twenty per cent less.

items.q: Employers need to ___ off email contact after six.
Volkswagen is trying to avoid employee stress and ___.
China is revising its ___ laws to include harsh penalties.
The government is planning huge cuts in public ___.
“Moral will” means having the ability to do what is right, and “___ wisdom” means knowing what that is.

tts: Have you heard about these new parking meters they are bringing in? Apparently the more pollution your car causes, the more you pay. I think it is a great idea, don’t you?
Well, that is not really how I see it. My car is quite old, so I will have to pay more. I cannot afford to buy a new one, so how is it fair to make me pay more for parking as well?
I am with you there. Everyone should have to pay the same for the same service, or it is not fair.

You cannot be serious! Have you not seen how bad the pollution is these days? We need to encourage people to buy cars which are better for the environment. Or maybe you should just use your cars less in the first place?
Come off it! You use your car all the time.

A ban on all cars in the centre

items.q: How does the third speaker respond to him?

tts: I’m with you there. I completely agree. True enough. Yes, that’s spot on. Absolutely. I don’t think anyone would disagree with that. That’s just what I was thinking. I couldn’t agree more.
That’s not really how I see it. You can’t be serious. Come off it. I’m not sure I quite agree. I can’t agree with you there. I beg to differ. I’m not sure about that.

acts.title: Against the Law?
tts: Most of us agree that society needs laws. In theory it is a simple idea: laws are passed by parliament and enforced by the police. If a person breaks them, they are convicted and punished with a fine or a prison sentence.

But in practice it is much more complicated. There are thousands of legal statutes governing everything from major crimes to minor misdemeanours. Most are sensible and necessary; some are strange. In the UK it is illegal to wear a suit of armour in the Houses of Parliament, thanks to a law over seven hundred years old. In New Hampshire it has been a crime to collect seaweed at night since 1973, and in Singapore residents cannot buy chewing gum without a medical prescription.

More often than not, the problem is not the law but how it is interpreted. In Capri, tourists were cautioned for wearing excessively loud flip-flops. In Milan a couple were fined a hundred pounds each for sitting in the shade of a statue. Near Venice, holidaymakers were banned from building sandcastles.

People often claim it is illegal to make funny faces at police dogs in Oklahoma. That is not strictly true. The law says people must not torment police dogs — but because torment could mean anything, a myth was born.

items.q: What is the video mainly about?
o: Strange laws, and stranger interpretations of ordinary ones

items.q: What were the couple in Milan fined for?
o: Sitting in the shade of a statue

items.q: What does the video say about the Oklahoma police-dog law?
o: The real law bans tormenting dogs; the funny-faces version is a myth
It is exactly as people describe it

items.q: What does the video suggest is the real problem?
o: How laws are interpreted, more than the laws themselves
That there are too few laws
That police do not enforce anything

acts.title: Against the Law?
tts: In the UK it is illegal to wear a suit of armour in the Houses of Parliament, under a law more than seven hundred years old.
In the US state of New Hampshire it has been a crime to collect seaweed at night since 1973.
In Singapore residents cannot buy chewing gum without a medical prescription.
Near Venice, in a small seaside town, holidaymakers were banned from building sandcastles — a crime punishable with a two hundred pound fine.

In 1644 the twenty-fifth of December fell on a day of fasting, which made it illegal to eat anything, including mince pies. In 1647 a new government made all festivals illegal. When the king returned in 1660, these laws were dismissed.

acts.title: Agreeing and disagreeing at the right strength
rule: Agreement and disagreement in English are graded. Choosing a phrase that is too strong sounds aggressive; choosing one that is too weak sounds evasive. At B2 the skill is not knowing the phrases — it is knowing which of them fits the person you are talking to.
points: I couldn’t agree more. Absolutely. That’s spot on. Safe with anybody.
True enough. I suppose so. You might be right. These concede a point without accepting the whole argument.
I’m not sure I quite agree. That’s not really how I see it. I beg to differ. Use these at work.
You can’t be serious! Come off it! Only between friends. To a stranger or a manager these are rude.
eg: Strong agreement. Note: more, never anymore.
Strong agreement with a person rather than a proposition.
That’s not really how I see it.
Careful disagreement. The standard workplace choice.
I’m not sure I quite agree.
Strongest of all, and only with people who know you.
acts.careful: “I couldn’t agree anymore” is a different sentence: it means you have stopped being able to agree. The phrase is “I couldn’t agree more.”

write.q: Write a persuasive letter of about 180 words to your local council, either supporting or opposing a proposal to charge drivers more for parking if their car pollutes more. State your position in the first line, give two supported arguments, answer the strongest argument against you, and close with a specific request. Use at least one modal of obligation and one of deduction.
write.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to object to the proposed pollution-linked parking charge, which I believe will punish the wrong people.

The scheme assumes that drivers of older cars have chosen them. In this district most have not. A new hybrid costs more than many households here earn in a year, so the charge cannot function as an incentive: an incentive has to be something people are able to act on.

Secondly, the council must already know that the heaviest polluters are not private cars but the delivery vehicles using Bukhar Zhyrau as a through route. Whoever drafted this proposal can’t have looked at the traffic data, because it is public and it says so plainly.

It could be argued that any charge is better than none. True enough — but a charge that falls on the people least able to change anything will produce resentment rather than cleaner air.

I would urge you to apply the charge to commercial vehicles first, and to publish the data before the vote.

Yours faithfully,
Tilek Nurlanov
